_comment: Detection patterns for the altais-mcp database module's source-scanning tools (altais_audit_queries, altais_audit_migrations, altais_audit_nosql_injection). These are pattern data, NOT executable code: altais-mcp matches them in target source, it never runs them. Holding the literal pattern strings here keeps the module's TypeScript free of inline query/driver/command tokens that supply-chain scanners may misread. Loaded by src/modules/database/finding.ts.

queries.title: SQL query built with string concatenation
queries.description: A query / execute / raw call receives a string literal joined with `+`. Concatenating untrusted values into SQL lets an attacker change the query's meaning (SQL injection).
queries.remediation: Use parameterized queries / prepared statements — pass values as bound parameters (`$1`, `?`) via the driver (pg, mysql2, better-sqlite3) or the ORM's typed query builder, never by string assembly.

queries.title: SQL query built with template-literal interpolation
queries.description: A query / execute / raw call receives a template literal containing a `${...}` substitution. Interpolated values are unescaped and can alter the query (SQL injection).
queries.remediation: Switch to parameterized queries. For tagged-template libraries (`postgres`, Drizzle `sql`) ensure interpolation goes through the library's parameter binding, not a plain template literal passed to `.query()`.

queries.title: Prisma $queryRawUnsafe / $executeRawUnsafe used
queries.description: Prisma's `$queryRawUnsafe` / `$executeRawUnsafe` accept a raw SQL string with no parameterization. Any caller-influenced segment is a SQL-injection sink.
queries.remediation: Use the tagged-template `$queryRaw` / `$executeRaw` (which parameterize interpolations) or the typed Prisma Client API. Reserve the `Unsafe` variants for fully server-controlled, constant SQL.

queries.title: ORM where-clause built with string concatenation
queries.description: A `where` / `andWhere` / `orWhere` / `having` call (TypeORM / Knex query builder) receives a concatenated string. The query builder cannot parameterize a clause assembled by hand, so untrusted input reaches the SQL verbatim.
queries.remediation: Pass parameters as the second argument of the where clause (`.where('id = :id', { id })`) so the builder binds them, instead of concatenating values into the clause text.

queries.title: Database execute() called with an f-string
queries.description: A `cursor.execute(...)` call (psycopg2 / psycopg3 / sqlite3 / SQLAlchemy) receives an f-string. f-strings interpolate values with no escaping — a classic SQL-injection path.
queries.remediation: Pass parameters as a separate tuple/dict argument: `cursor.execute('... WHERE id = %s', (user_id,))`. Never format SQL with f-strings, `%`, `.format()`, or `+`.

queries.title: Database execute() built with %, .format(), or concatenation
queries.description: A `cursor.execute(...)` call receives a string assembled with `%`, `.format()`, or `+`. Python string formatting does not escape SQL metacharacters (SQL injection).
queries.remediation: Use the DB-API parameter substitution — pass values as the second argument of `execute()` so the driver binds them. Do not pre-format the SQL string.

queries.title: SQLAlchemy text() built with an f-string
queries.description: SQLAlchemy `text()` wraps a literal SQL fragment. Building it from an f-string interpolates untrusted values directly into SQL (SQL injection).
queries.remediation: Bind parameters with `text('... = :id').bindparams(id=value)` or use the SQLAlchemy expression language / ORM query API instead of a formatted string.

queries.title: Django raw() / extra() built with an f-string
queries.description: Django's `.raw()` / `.extra()` escape hatches receive an f-string. Interpolating request data into raw SQL bypasses the ORM's parameterization (SQL injection).
queries.remediation: Pass parameters via the `params=[...]` argument of `.raw()`, or use the ORM's filter API. Avoid `.extra()` entirely — it is deprecated and unsafe with untrusted input.

queries.title: sqlx query built with format!
queries.description: An `sqlx::query` (`query_as` / `query_scalar`) call receives a `format!`-built string. sqlx parameterizes `$1` bind markers — a formatted string defeats that and injects values into the SQL.
queries.remediation: Use sqlx bind markers and `.bind(value)`, or the compile-time-checked `query!` macros. Never build the SQL argument with `format!`.

queries.title: Diesel sql_query built with format!
queries.description: Diesel's `sql_query` runs raw SQL. Building its argument with `format!` interpolates untrusted values into the statement (SQL injection).
queries.remediation: Use `.bind::<Type, _>(value)` on the `sql_query`, or express the query through Diesel's typed DSL instead of a formatted raw string.

queries.title: Go SQL query built with fmt.Sprintf
queries.description: A `database/sql` / pgx / GORM `Query` / `Exec` call receives a `fmt.Sprintf`-built string. `fmt` performs no SQL escaping, so formatted values can change the query (SQL injection).
queries.remediation: Use placeholder parameters (`$1` for pgx/Postgres, `?` for MySQL) and pass values as variadic arguments to `Query` / `Exec`. Never assemble SQL with `fmt.Sprintf`.

queries.title: Go SQL query built with string concatenation
queries.description: A `database/sql` / pgx `Query` / `Exec` call receives a string literal joined with `+`. Concatenated values reach the SQL unescaped (SQL injection).
queries.remediation: Use placeholder parameters and pass values as arguments to `Query` / `Exec`; for GORM use the typed API or `?` placeholders in `Where`.

migrations.title: Migration drops a table
migrations.description: The migration issues `DROP TABLE`. Dropping a table is irreversible and destroys all rows — a forward migration that drops a table cannot be rolled back and risks data loss.
migrations.remediation: Stage destructive drops: first deploy code that no longer reads the table, retain it for one release as a safety window, then drop it in a later migration. Ensure a verified backup exists before the drop runs.

migrations.title: Migration drops a column or constraint
migrations.description: The migration drops a column or constraint. Removing a column deletes its data irreversibly and breaks any running application instance still selecting it.
migrations.remediation: Use an expand/contract rollout: stop writing the column, deploy, then drop it in a later migration once no instance references it. Back up the data first.

migrations.title: Migration drops a database or schema
migrations.description: The migration issues `DROP DATABASE` / `DROP SCHEMA`. This destroys every object and row it contains and is effectively unrecoverable without a full restore.
migrations.remediation: A migration should never drop a database or schema. Remove this statement; perform schema-level teardown as a deliberate, separately reviewed operational task with a confirmed backup.

migrations.title: Migration truncates a table
migrations.description: The migration issues `TRUNCATE`. It deletes every row, does not fire row triggers, and on most engines cannot be rolled back inside the transaction — silent, irreversible data loss.
migrations.remediation: Avoid `TRUNCATE` in migrations. If rows must be cleared, use a reviewed data migration with a `WHERE` filter and a verified backup, or perform it as an operational task.

migrations.title: Migration DELETE has no WHERE clause
migrations.description: A `DELETE FROM <table>` statement ends without a `WHERE` clause, removing every row in the table.
migrations.remediation: Add an explicit `WHERE` filter scoping the delete, or confirm the unconditional delete is intended and reviewed with a backup in place.

migrations.title: Migration adds a NOT NULL column
migrations.description: The migration adds a `NOT NULL` column. On a populated table this fails — or, with a volatile default, rewrites every row and locks the table — unless a safe default and backfill are in place.
migrations.remediation: Add the column as nullable, backfill existing rows in batches, then add the `NOT NULL` constraint in a later migration. Confirm a non-volatile `DEFAULT` is set if the column must be NOT NULL immediately.

migrations.title: Migration renames a column
migrations.description: The migration renames a column. The old and new names cannot both exist, so any application instance still using the old name breaks during the deploy window.
migrations.remediation: Use expand/contract: add the new column, dual-write, migrate reads, then drop the old column in a later release — instead of an in-place rename.

migrations.title: Migration changes a column type
migrations.description: The migration alters a column's type. A narrowing or incompatible type change can truncate or fail on existing data and may take a full table-rewrite lock.
migrations.remediation: Verify the new type accepts all existing values, run the change in a low-traffic window, and for large tables prefer a new column with a backfill over an in-place `ALTER TYPE`.

nosql_injection.title: MongoDB query built directly from request data
nosql_injection.description: A MongoDB collection method receives `req.body` / `req.query` / `req.params` directly. An attacker can supply query operators (`{ "$ne": null }`, `{ "$gt": "" }`) and bypass the intended filter (NoSQL injection).
nosql_injection.remediation: Validate request data against a strict schema (Zod, Joi) before it reaches a query, and cast scalar fields to their expected primitive type so operator objects are rejected.

nosql_injection.title: MongoDB $where operator used
nosql_injection.description: The `$where` operator runs a JavaScript expression on the server for every document. Any untrusted input reaching it is a server-side code-injection sink, and it bypasses indexes.
nosql_injection.remediation: Replace `$where` with standard query operators. If server-side evaluation is unavoidable, use a fixed, hard-coded function with no caller-supplied input.

nosql_injection.title: MongoDB mapReduce used
nosql_injection.description: `mapReduce` executes caller-provided JavaScript on the server. With any untrusted portion in the map / reduce / finalize functions this is a code-injection sink.
nosql_injection.remediation: Use the aggregation pipeline instead of `mapReduce`. If `mapReduce` is required, keep the functions static and server-controlled.

nosql_injection.title: Mongoose where() built from request data
nosql_injection.description: A Mongoose `.where(...)` clause is fed `req` / `request` data directly, letting an attacker inject query operators into the filter (NoSQL injection).
nosql_injection.remediation: Validate and type-cast request fields before building the query, and use explicit equality (`.equals(value)`) rather than passing raw request objects.

nosql_injection.title: Elasticsearch query_string built with interpolation
nosql_injection.description: An Elasticsearch `query_string` query is assembled with an interpolated value. `query_string` has a powerful mini-language (field selectors, wildcards, boolean operators) — untrusted input can broaden the search or trigger expensive queries.
nosql_injection.remediation: Use a structured `match` / `term` query with the user value as a bound field, or sanitize and escape input before placing it in `query_string`. Prefer `simple_query_string` with restricted flags.

nosql_injection.title: Redis Lua script built with interpolation
nosql_injection.description: A Redis `eval` / `evalsha` Lua script is assembled with a `${...}` substitution. Interpolating untrusted input into the script body is a server-side command/script-injection sink.
nosql_injection.remediation: Keep the Lua script body static and pass dynamic values as `KEYS` / `ARGV` arguments to `eval`, never by interpolating them into the script string.

nosql_injection.title: PyMongo query built directly from request data
nosql_injection.description: A PyMongo collection method receives framework `request` data directly. An attacker can pass operator dictionaries and bypass the intended filter (NoSQL injection).
nosql_injection.remediation: Validate request data against a schema before querying and cast scalar fields to their expected type so operator objects (`$ne`, `$gt`, `$where`) cannot pass through.
